title: A Bottle of Dew — Class 6 CBSE English
subject: English

slides.title: A Bottle of Dew
bullets: Class 6 — CBSE English
Poorvi · Chapter 1 · Unit: Fables and Folk Tales
slides.speaker_notes: Welcome students. Stories that teach us are called fables; this one is short, simple and powerful.

slides.title: What you'll be able to do
bullets: Retell the story in your own words.
Identify characters, plot and moral.
Use new vocabulary correctly.
Spot common nouns, proper nouns, adjectives.
Use the past tense in narrative.
slides.speaker_notes: Read each; ask which is hardest.

slides.title: What is a fable?
bullets: A short story with a hidden lesson — the MORAL.
Often features simple characters or animals.
Comes from oral storytelling tradition.
The moral is the BIG idea you take away.
'A Bottle of Dew' is a fable in the spirit of folk tales.
slides.speaker_notes: Distinguish fable from fairy tale or fantasy.

slides.title: The story
bullets: A wise old king gathers his people in the courtyard.
He holds up an empty crystal bottle.
'Bring me the most precious thing in the world to fill it.'
The next morning, four villagers come — three adults and a child.
Each brings something different.
slides.speaker_notes: Read with feeling; pause at the king's question.

slides.title: Four offerings
bullets: Goldsmith: a tiny bag of GOLD DUST.
Poet: a few WORDS written on paper.
Farmer: a single GRAIN OF RICE.
Child: a leaf with a DROP OF DEW.
Each reflects what that person values most.
slides.speaker_notes: Have students predict which offering will win before revealing.

slides.title: The child's wisdom
bullets: 'Look, your majesty,' said the child.
'It came from the morning. It came from nowhere.'
'It will be gone in a moment.'
'But while it is here, it is the most precious thing of all — because it is now.'
The king smiles.
slides.speaker_notes: Stress the words 'because it is NOW' — that is the moral.

slides.title: The moral
bullets: Gold can be saved.
Words can be remembered.
Rice can be stored.
But a moment cannot be brought back.
The PRESENT MOMENT is the most precious thing of all.
slides.speaker_notes: Make sure students articulate the moral in their own words.

slides.title: Vocabulary you should know
bullets: precious — valuable; not common.
thankful — grateful.
delicately — gently, carefully.
courtyard — open space inside / beside a building.
dew — early-morning water drops on leaves.
slides.speaker_notes: Use each word in a sentence on the board.

slides.title: Language: nouns and adjectives
bullets: COMMON noun: names a class — king, child, leaf.
PROPER noun: names a particular thing; capital letter — Aesop, Mumbai.
ADJECTIVE: describes a noun — wise, crystal, small.
Example: 'a SMALL child held a BRIGHT leaf.'
Find the adjectives → small, bright.

slides.title: Language: past tense
bullets: Stories are usually told in the past tense.
Regular verbs add -ed: walk → walked; smile → smiled.
Irregular verbs change form: bring → brought; see → saw; keep → kept.
From the story: gathered, brought, smiled, held, kept.
Practice: convert 'I see the king' to past — 'I SAW the king'.

slides.title: Practising language: pick out the parts
bullets: 'A small child held a bright green leaf delicately.'
Adjectives: small, bright, green.
Verb (past tense): held.
Common noun: child, leaf.
Adverb (extra): delicately.

slides.title: You try (5 minutes)
bullets: 1. What did the goldsmith bring? Why?
2. Use 'precious' in your own sentence.
3. Convert 'I bring a flower' to past tense.
4. Pick out one common noun and one adjective from: 'The wise king sat on a golden throne.'
5. State the moral in your own words.

slides.title: Quick check
bullets: Q1. Who brings the dew?
Q2. Past tense of 'see'?
Q3. Synonym of precious?
Q4. Common or proper: 'child'?
Show your answers on fingers.

slides.title: Key takeaways
bullets: A fable carries a moral inside a story.
Four characters bring four offerings; the child's wisdom wins.
Moral: the PRESENT moment is most precious.
Vocabulary: precious, thankful, delicately, courtyard, dew.
Common vs proper nouns; adjectives; past-tense verbs.
Apply the moral to your own life — that is what fables are for.
slides.speaker_notes: Hand out worksheet; announce homework on a 'precious moment' from one's own life.
